{{short description|Quaternions with complex number coefficients}}
In [[abstract algebra]], the '''biquaternions''' are the numbers {{math|''w'' + ''x'' '''i''' + ''y'' '''j''' + ''z'' '''k'''}}, where {{math|''w'', ''x'', ''y''}}, and {{mvar|z}} are [[complex number]]s, or variants thereof, and the elements of {{math|{{mset|'''1''', '''i''', '''j''', '''k'''}}}} multiply as in the [[quaternion group]] and commute with their coefficients. There are three types of biquaternions corresponding to complex numbers and the variations thereof:
* Biquaternions when the coefficients are [[complex number]]s.
* [[Split-biquaternion]]s when the coefficients are [[split-complex number]]s.
* [[Dual quaternion]]s when the coefficients are [[dual numbers]].

This article is about the ''ordinary biquaternions'' named by [[William Rowan Hamilton]] in 1844.{{sfn|Hamilton|1850}} Some of the more prominent proponents of these biquaternions include [[Alexander Macfarlane]], [[Arthur W. Conway]], [[Ludwik Silberstein]], and [[Cornelius Lanczos]]. As developed below, the unit [[quasi-sphere]] of the biquaternions provides a representation of the [[Lorentz group]], which is the foundation of [[special relativity]].

The algebra of biquaternions can be considered as a [[tensor product of algebras|tensor product]] {{math|'''C''' ⊗<sub>'''R'''</sub> '''H'''}}, where {{math|'''C'''}} is the [[field (mathematics)|field]] of complex numbers and {{math|'''H'''}} is the [[division algebra]] of (real) [[quaternions]]. In other words, the biquaternions are just the [[complexification]] of the quaternions. Viewed as a complex algebra, the biquaternions are isomorphic to the algebra of {{math|2 × 2}} complex matrices {{math|M<sub>2</sub>('''C''')}}.  They are also isomorphic to several [[Clifford algebra]]s including {{math|1={{math|'''C''' ⊗<sub>'''R'''</sub> '''H'''}} = Cl{{su|b=3|p=[0]|lh=0.9em}}('''C''') = Cl<sub>2</sub>('''C''') = Cl<sub>1,2</sub>('''R''')}},{{sfn|Garling|2011|pp=112,113}} the [[Pauli algebra]] {{math|Cl<sub>3,0</sub>('''R''')}},{{sfn|Garling|2011|p=112}}{{sfn|Francis|Kosowsky|2005|p=404}} and the even part {{math|1=Cl{{su|b=1,3|p=[0]|lh=0.9em}}('''R''') = Cl{{su|b=3,1|p=[0]|lh=0.9em}}('''R''')}} of the [[spacetime algebra]].{{sfn|Francis|Kosowsky|2005|p=386}} In the [[physics]] literature, the biquaternions, in its real Clifford algebra definition as {{math|Cl<sub>3,0</sub>('''R''')}}, are used under the name [[algebra of physical space]].<ref name="Sobczyk2019">{{cite book |last1=Sobczyk |first1=Garret |title=Matrix Gateway to Geometric Algebra, Spacetime and Spinors |date=2 November 2019 |publisher=Amazon Distribution GmbH |isbn=9781704596624}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let {{math|{'''1''', '''i''', '''j''', '''k'''<nowiki>}</nowiki>}} be the basis for the (real) [[quaternion]]s {{math|'''H'''}}, and let {{math|''u'', ''v'', ''w'', ''x''}} be complex numbers, then
: <math>q = u \mathbf 1 + v \mathbf i + w \mathbf j + x \mathbf k</math>
is a ''biquaternion''.{{sfn|Hamilton|1853|p=639}} To distinguish square roots of minus one in the biquaternions, Hamilton{{sfn|Hamilton|1853|p=730}}{{sfn|Hamilton|1866|p=289}} and [[Arthur W. Conway]] used the convention of representing the square root of minus one in the scalar field {{math|'''C'''}} by {{math|''h''}} to avoid confusion with the {{math|'''i'''}} in the quaternion group. [[Commutativity]] of the scalar field with the quaternion group is assumed:
: <math> h \mathbf i = \mathbf i h,\ \ h \mathbf j = \mathbf j h,\ \ h \mathbf k = \mathbf k h .</math>

Hamilton introduced the terms ''[[bivector (complex)|bivector]]'', ''biconjugate'', ''bitensor'', and ''biversor'' to extend notions used with real quaternions {{math|'''H'''}}.

Hamilton's primary exposition on biquaternions came in 1853 in his ''Lectures on Quaternions''. The editions of ''Elements of Quaternions'', in 1866 by [[William Edwin Hamilton]] (son of Rowan), and in 1899, 1901 by [[Charles Jasper Joly]], reduced the biquaternion coverage in favour of the real quaternions.

Considered with the operations of component-wise addition, and multiplication according to the quaternion group, this collection forms a [[Four-dimensional space|4-dimensional]] [[algebra over a field|algebra]] over the complex numbers {{math|'''C'''}}. The algebra of biquaternions is [[associative]], but not [[commutative]]. A biquaternion is either a [[unit (ring theory)|unit]] or a [[zero divisor]]. The algebra of biquaternions forms a [[composition algebra]] and can be constructed from [[bicomplex number]]s. See ''{{section link||As a composition algebra}}'' below.

== Place in ring theory ==

=== Linear representation ===
Note that the [[matrix product]]
: <math>\begin{pmatrix}h & 0\\0 & -h\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & h\\h & 0\end{pmatrix}</math>.

Because {{math|''h''}} is the [[imaginary unit]], each of these three arrays has a square equal to the negative of the [[identity matrix]].
When this matrix product is interpreted as {{math|1='''i''' '''j''' = '''k'''}}, then one obtains a [[subgroup]] of matrices that is [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[quaternion group]]. Consequently,
: <math>\begin{pmatrix}u+hv & w+hx\\-w+hx & u-hv\end{pmatrix}</math>
represents biquaternion {{math|1=''q'' = ''u'' '''1''' + ''v'' '''i''' + ''w'' '''j''' + ''x'' '''k'''}}.
Given any {{math|2 × 2}} complex matrix, there are complex values {{math|''u''}}, {{math|''v''}}, {{math|''w''}}, and {{math|''x''}} to put it in this form so that the [[matrix ring]] {{math|M(2, '''C''')}} is isomorphic{{sfn|Dickson|1914|p=13}} to the biquaternion [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]. This representation also shows that the 16-element group
: <math>\{\pm\mathbf 1, \pm h, \pm\mathbf i, \pm h\mathbf i, \pm\mathbf j, \pm h\mathbf j, \pm\mathbf k, \pm h\mathbf k \}</math>
is isomorphic to the [[Pauli group]], the [[central product]] of a [[cyclic group]] of order 4 and the [[dihedral group]] of order 8. Concretely, the [[Pauli matrices]]
:<math>X = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0&-h\\
h&0
\end{pmatrix},\quad
Z =
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&-1
\end{pmatrix}</math>
correspond respectively to the elements {{math|－''h'''''k''', －''h'''''j'''}}, and {{math|－''h'''''i'''}}.

=== Subalgebras ===
Considering the biquaternion algebra over the scalar field of real numbers {{math|'''R'''}}, the set
: <math>\{\mathbf 1, h, \mathbf i, h\mathbf i, \mathbf j, h\mathbf j, \mathbf k, h\mathbf k \}</math>
forms a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] so the algebra has eight real [[dimension]]s. The squares of the elements {{math|''h'''''i''', ''h'''''j'''}}, and {{math|''h'''''k'''}} are all positive one, for example, {{math|1=(''h'''''i''')<sup>2</sup> = ''h''<sup>2</sup>'''i'''<sup>2</sup> = (−'''1''')(−'''1''') = +'''1'''}}.

The [[subalgebra]] given by
: <math>\{ x + y(h\mathbf i) : x, y \in \R \} </math>
is [[ring isomorphism|ring isomorphic]] to the plane of [[split-complex number]]s, which has an algebraic structure built upon the [[unit hyperbola]]. The elements {{math|''h'''''j'''}} and {{math|''h'''''k'''}} also determine such subalgebras.

Furthermore, <math>\{ x + y \mathbf j : x,y \in \Complex \} </math> is a subalgebra isomorphic to the [[bicomplex number]]s.

A third subalgebra called [[coquaternion]]s is generated by {{math|''h'''''j'''}} and {{math|''h'''''k'''}}. It is seen that {{math|1=(''h'''''j''')(''h'''''k''') = (−'''1''')'''i'''}}, and that the square of this element is {{math|−'''1'''}}. These elements generate the [[dihedral group]] of the square. The [[linear subspace]] with basis {{math|{'''1''', '''i''', ''h'''''j''', ''h'''''k'''<nowiki>}</nowiki>}} thus is closed under multiplication, and forms the coquaternion algebra.

In the context of [[quantum mechanics]] and [[spinor]] algebra, the biquaternions {{math|''h'''''i''', ''h'''''j'''}}, and {{math|''h'''''k'''}} (or their negatives), viewed in the {{math|M<sub>2</sub>('''C''')}} representation, are called [[Pauli matrices]].

== Algebraic properties ==
The biquaternions have two ''conjugations'':
* the '''biconjugate''' or biscalar minus [[bivector (complex)|bivector]] is <math>q^* = w - x\mathbf i - y\mathbf j - z\mathbf k \!\ ,</math> and
* the [[complex conjugation]] of biquaternion coefficients <math>\bar{q} = \bar{w} + \bar{x}\mathbf i + \bar{y} \mathbf j + \bar{z}\mathbf k </math>
where <math>\bar{z} = a - bh</math> when <math>z = a + bh,\quad a,b \in \reals,\quad h^2 = -\mathbf 1.</math>

Note that <math>(pq)^* = q^* p^*, \quad \overline{pq} = \bar{p} \bar{q}, \quad \overline{q^*} = \bar{q}^*.</math>

Clearly, if <math>q q^* = 0 </math> then {{math|''q''}} is a zero divisor. Otherwise <math>\lbrace q q^* \rbrace^{-\mathbf 1} </math> is a complex number. Further, <math>q q^* = q^* q </math> is easily verified. This allows the inverse to be defined by
* <math>q^{-1} = q^* \lbrace q q^* \rbrace^{-1}</math>, if <math>qq^* \neq 0.</math>

=== Relation to Lorentz transformations ===
{{Further||History of Lorentz transformations}}

Consider now the linear subspace{{sfn|Lanczos|1949|loc=See equation 94.16, page 305. The following algebra compares to Lanczos, except he uses ~ to signify quaternion conjugation and * for complex conjugation}}
: <math>M = \lbrace q\colon q^* = \bar{q} \rbrace = \lbrace t + x(h\mathbf i) + y(h \mathbf j) + z(h \mathbf k)\colon t, x, y, z \in \reals \rbrace .</math>

{{math|''M''}} is not a subalgebra since it is not [[closure (mathematics)|closed under products]]; for example <math>(h\mathbf i)(h\mathbf j) = h^2 \mathbf{ij} = -\mathbf k \notin M.</math> Indeed, {{math|''M''}} cannot form an algebra if it is not even a [[magma (algebra)|magma]].

'''Proposition:''' If {{mvar|q}} is in {{mvar|M}}, then <math>q q^* = t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2.</math>

Proof: From the definitions,
: <math>\begin{align}
q q^* &= (t+xh\mathbf i+yh\mathbf j+zh\mathbf k)(t-xh\mathbf i-yh\mathbf j-zh\mathbf k)\\
&= t^2 - x^2(h\mathbf i)^2 - y^2(h\mathbf j)^2 - z^2(h\mathbf k)^2 \\
&= t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2.
\end{align} </math>

'''Definition:''' Let biquaternion {{mvar|g}} satisfy <math>g g^* = 1.</math> Then the [[Lorentz transformation]] associated with {{mvar|g}} is given by
: <math>T(q) = g^* q \bar{g}.</math>

'''Proposition:''' If {{mvar|q}} is in {{mvar|M}}, then {{math|''T''(''q'')}} is also in {{math|''M''}}.

Proof: <math>(g^* q \bar{g})^* = \bar{g}^* q^* g = \overline{g^*} \bar{q} g = \overline{g^* q \bar{g})}.</math>

'''Proposition:''' <math>\quad T(q) (T(q))^* = q q^* </math>

Proof: Note first that ''gg''* = 1 implies that the sum of the squares of its four complex components is one. Then the sum of the squares of the ''complex conjugates'' of these components is also one. Therefore, <math>\bar{g} (\bar{g})^* =  1.</math> Now
: <math>(g^* q \bar{g})(g^* q \bar{g})^* = g^* q (\bar{g} \bar{g}^*) q^* g = g^* q q^* g = q q^*.</math>

== Associated terminology ==
As the biquaternions have been a fixture of [[linear algebra]] since the beginnings of [[mathematical physics]], there is an array of concepts that are illustrated or represented by biquaternion algebra. The [[transformation group]] <math>G = \lbrace g : g g^* = 1 \rbrace </math> has two parts, <math>G \cap H</math>  and <math>G \cap M.</math> The first part is characterized by <math>g = \bar{g}</math> ; then the Lorentz transformation corresponding to {{mvar|g}} is given by <math>T(q) = g^{-1} q g </math> since <math>g^* = g^{-1}. </math> Such a transformation is a [[quaternions and spatial rotation|rotation by quaternion multiplication]], and the collection of them is {{math|[[SO(3)]]}} <math>\cong G \cap H .</math> But this subgroup of {{mvar|G}} is not a [[normal subgroup]], so no [[quotient group]] can be formed.

To view <math>G \cap M</math> it is necessary to show some subalgebra structure in the biquaternions. Let {{mvar|r}} represent an element of the [[quaternion#Square roots of −1|sphere of square roots of minus one]] in the real quaternion subalgebra {{math|'''H'''}}. Then {{math|1=(''hr'')<sup>2</sup> = +1}} and the plane of biquaternions given by <math>D_r = \lbrace z = x + yhr : x, y \in \mathbb R \rbrace</math> is a commutative subalgebra isomorphic to the plane of split-complex numbers. Just as the ordinary complex plane has a unit circle, <math>D_r </math> has a [[unit hyperbola]] given by
: <math>\exp(ahr) = \cosh(a) + hr\ \sinh(a),\quad a \in R. </math>

Just as the unit circle turns by multiplication through one of its elements, so the hyperbola turns because <math>\exp(ahr) \exp(bhr) = \exp((a+b)hr). </math> Hence these algebraic operators on the hyperbola are called [[versor#Hyperbolic versor|hyperbolic versors]]. The unit circle in {{math|'''C'''}} and unit hyperbola in {{math|''D''<sub>''r''</sub>}} are examples of [[one-parameter group]]s. For every square root {{math|''r''}} of minus one in {{math|'''H'''}}, there is a one-parameter group in the biquaternions given by <math>G \cap D_r.</math>

The space of biquaternions has a natural [[topology]] through the [[Euclidean metric]] on {{math|8}}-space. With respect to this topology, {{mvar|G}} is a [[topological group]]. Moreover, it has analytic structure making it a six-parameter [[Lie group]]. Consider the subspace of bivectors  <math>A = \lbrace q : q^* = -q \rbrace </math>. Then the [[exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential map]]
<math>\exp:A \to G</math>  takes the real vectors to <math>G \cap H</math> and the {{mvar|h}}-vectors to <math>G \cap M.</math> When equipped with the [[commutator]], {{mvar|A}} forms the [[Lie algebra]] of {{mvar|G}}. Thus this study of a [[six-dimensional space]] serves to introduce the general concepts of [[Lie theory]]. When viewed in the matrix representation, {{mvar|G}} is called the [[special linear group]] {{math|[[SL(2,C)]]}} in {{math|M(2, '''C''')}}.

Many of the concepts of [[special relativity]] are illustrated through the biquaternion structures laid out. The subspace {{mvar|M}} corresponds to [[Minkowski space]], with the four coordinates giving the time and space locations of events in a resting [[frame of reference]]. Any hyperbolic versor {{math|exp(''ahr'')}} corresponds to a [[velocity]] in direction {{mvar|r}} of speed {{math|''c'' tanh ''a''}}  where {{mvar|c}} is the [[velocity of light]]. The inertial frame of reference of this velocity can be made the resting frame by applying the [[Lorentz boost]] {{mvar|T}} given by {{math|1=''g'' = exp(0.5''ahr'')}} since then <math>g^{\star} = \exp(-0.5ahr) = g^*</math> so that <math>T(\exp(ahr)) = 1 .</math>
Naturally the [[hyperboloid]] <math>G \cap M,</math> which represents the range of velocities for sub-luminal motion, is of physical interest. There has been considerable work associating this "velocity space" with the [[hyperboloid model]] of [[hyperbolic geometry]].  In special relativity, the [[hyperbolic angle]] parameter of a hyperbolic versor is called [[rapidity]]. Thus we see the biquaternion group {{mvar|G}} provides a [[group representation]] for the [[Lorentz group]].{{sfn|Hermann|1974|loc=chapter 6.4 Complex Quaternions and Maxwell's Equations}}

After the introduction of [[spinor]] theory, particularly in the hands of [[Wolfgang Pauli]] and [[Élie Cartan]], the biquaternion representation of the Lorentz group was superseded. The new methods were founded on [[basis (linear algebra)|basis vectors]] in the set
: <math>\{ q \ :\  q q^* = 0 \} = \left\{ w + x\mathbf i + y\mathbf j + z\mathbf k \ :\ w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 0 \right\} </math>

which is called the ''complex light cone''. The above [[Representation theory of the Lorentz group|representation of the Lorentz group]] coincides with what physicists refer to as [[four-vector]]s.  Beyond four-vectors, the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics also includes other Lorentz representations, known as [[Lorentz scalar|scalars]], and the {{math|(1, 0) ⊕ (0, 1)}}-representation associated with e.g. the [[electromagnetic field tensor]]. Furthermore, particle physics makes use of the {{math|SL(2, '''C''')}} representations (or [[projective representation]]s of the Lorentz group) known as left- and right-handed [[Weyl spinor]]s, [[Majorana spinor]]s, and [[Dirac spinor]]s.  It is known that each of these seven representations can be constructed as invariant subspaces within the biquaternions.{{sfn|Furey|2012}}

== As a composition algebra ==
Although W. R. Hamilton introduced biquaternions in the 19th century, its delineation of its [[mathematical structure]] as a special type of [[algebra over a field]] was accomplished in the 20th century: the biquaternions may be generated out of the [[bicomplex number]]s in the same way that [[Adrian Albert]] generated the real quaternions out of complex numbers in the so-called [[Cayley–Dickson construction]].  In this construction, a bicomplex number {{math|(''w'', ''z'')}} has conjugate {{math|1=(''w'', ''z'')* = (''w'', – ''z'')}}.

The biquaternion is then a pair of bicomplex numbers {{math|(''a'', ''b'')}}, where the product with a second biquaternion {{math|(''c'', ''d'')}} is
: <math>(a,b)(c,d) = (a c - d^* b, d a + b c^* ).</math>

If <math>a = (u, v), b = (w,z), </math> then the ''biconjugate'' <math>(a, b)^* = (a^*, -b).</math>

When {{math|(''a'', ''b'')*}} is written as a 4-vector of ordinary complex numbers,
: <math>(u, v, w, z)^* = (u, -v, -w, -z). </math>
The biquaternions form an example of a [[quaternion algebra]], and it has norm
: <math>N(u,v,w,z) = u^2 + v^2 + w^2 + z^2 .</math>
Two biquaternions {{math|''p''}} and {{math|''q''}} satisfy {{math|1=''N''(''pq'') = ''N''(''p'') ''N''(''q'')}}, indicating that {{math|''N''}} is a quadratic form admitting composition, so that the biquaternions form a [[composition algebra]].

== Scalar-vector representation ==
An arbitrary biquaternion <math>A</math> can be represented as a sum of a complex
number (''scalar'') <math>\alpha = Sc(A)</math>
and a three-dimensional complex-valued vector <math>\mathbf a = Vc(A)</math><ref>L. Silberstein, ''Quaternionic Form of Relativity'', Philos. Mag. S., 6, Vol. 23, No. 137, pp. 790-809, 1912.</ref>:

: <math>A = \alpha + \mathbf a = (\alpha,\mathbf a)</math>

There are two types of scalar-vector representation, based on different forms of biquaternionic product. Both representations are equivalent. In  ''standard representation''<ref>A. A. Alekseeva, ''Differential Algebra of Biquaternions. Lorentz Transformations of Biwave Equations'', Mathematical Journal, Almaty, Vol. 10, No. 35, 2010, pp. 33-41</ref> the product of two biquaternions <math>A = (\alpha,\mathbf a)</math> and <math>B = (\beta,\mathbf b)</math>
has the form:

: <math>A B = (\alpha \beta - (\mathbf a \mathbf b),\alpha \mathbf b + \beta \mathbf a + [\mathbf a \mathbf b])</math>,

where <math>(\mathbf a \mathbf b)</math> and <math>[\mathbf a \mathbf b]</math> are [[dot product|scalar product]] and [[cross product|vector product]]  of <math>\mathbf a</math> and <math>\mathbf b</math>, respectively. 
In ''complex representation''<ref>S.Ya. Kotkovsky, "Nullvector Algebra", Hypercomplex Numbers in Geometry and Physics, 12:2(23), 2015, pp. 59-172</ref> the product of the same biquaternions  has the form:

: <math>A B = (\alpha \beta + (\mathbf a \mathbf b),\alpha \mathbf b + \beta \mathbf a + i [\mathbf a \mathbf b])</math>

Note that in complex representation the product of two real-valued biquaternions yields a complex-valued biquaternion unless their vector parts are collinear. ''Biquaternionic conjugate'' of a given biquaternion <math>A=(\alpha,\mathbf a)</math> is defined as:
: <math>\overline A = (\alpha, - \mathbf a)</math>

''Square modulus'' of a biquaternion <math>A=(\alpha,\mathbf a)</math> is a complex number

: <math>|A|^2 = A \overline A = \overline A A = \alpha^2 - \mathbf a^2</math>

The latter has the multiplicative property:

: <math>|A B|^2 = |A|^2 |B|^2</math>

Applying biquaternonic or complex conjugation to the product of biquaternions turns each multiplier to its conjugate and change their order:
: <math>\overline { A B } = \overline B \overline A</math>
: <math>( A B )^* = B^* A^*</math>

Depending on their square modulus, all biquaternions are divided into two non-intersecting subspaces (by multiplication): nullquaternions and finite biquaternions. Nullquaternions are biquaternions with zero square modulus; finite biquaternions are biquaternions with non-zero square modulus.
